sources.title: Han Xuhui, study of female musician figurines and dress, Chinese National Arts and Crafts Society (2025)
sources.note: Direct article and exact indexed section 3.2 read. Main subject is Later Shu; only comparative Feng Hui tomb at Binxian, dated 958, used here. East-wall towel and spittoon attendants, west-wall cushion attendant. Disputed reconstruction of undergarments not adopted.

sources.title: Donald B. Wagner, The Cast Iron Lion of Cangzhou (Needham Research Institute, 1991)
sources.note: Author’s direct full text, newsletter 10 pp. 2-3, web revisions 2022/2024. Cast 953; height 5.4 m; piece mould, staged pours, reinforcing pegs. Weight estimates and speculative removal of a bronze bodhisattva omitted, as is erroneous Shizong reign endpoint in incidental sentence.

sources.title: Fitzwilliam Museum, Zhou Yuan Tong Bao, CM.294-2015
sources.note: Direct object catalogue: copper one-cash coin, 955-960, 23.67 mm, 2.75 g, obverse 周元通寶, translation Zhou First Currency, crescent above reverse hole. Catalogue ruler field incorrectly implies 955-960 reign; public date is explicitly the object catalogue range, not Shizong’s reign. No archaeological findspot or visual facsimile verified.

sources.title: Jeffrey Moser, Nominal Things: Bronzes in the Making of Medieval China (2023)

proposedOverrides.name: Later Zhou
proposedOverrides.summary: The final Five Dynasties regime, whose central military and administrative reforms preceded Song rule.

index.name: Later Jin
index.summary: The third of the Five Dynasties, set up by Shi Jingtang as a client of the Khitan Liao, to whom he ceded the Sixteen Prefectures.

fell.text: The Liao sacked Kaifeng in 947 and carried off the emperor; Liu Zhiyuan then took the throne as founder of the Later Han.

index.name: Later Han
index.summary: The shortest of the Five Dynasties, four years under the Shatuo general Liu Zhiyuan and his son.

fell.text: The general Guo Wei took Kaifeng in 951 and founded the Later Zhou.

index.name: Later Zhou
index.summary: The last of the Five Dynasties, whose emperor Shizong rebuilt the army and the treasury and began the reconquest of the south that the Song completed.

fell.text: The army proclaimed its general Zhao Kuangyin emperor at Chenqiao in 960; he founded the Song.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: One exact uncovered seams ID; no aliases. Ancient Zhou, Later Tang, Later Han, Later Jin and Song remain distinct records.
batchIdentityNotes.geography: China-seams.geojson site-created coarse polygon, 951-960, bounds 102-122 E / 32-40 N; source explicitly says not a surveyed boundary. Public caution retained. No claim that all its area was held throughout this interval or that China was reunified.
batchIdentityNotes.chronology: Historical reign interval 951-960 preserved. Feng Hui died 952; tomb paintings are dated 958 in the cited study, so death and decoration dates are not conflated. Fitzwilliam object dated 955-960, but Shizong himself reigned 954-959.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Contemporary copper cash inscription 周元通寶 with museum translation Zhou First Currency. Modern typesetting and modern Mandarin pinyin explicitly identified. No reconstructed period pronunciation.
batchIdentityNotes.limitations: No independently supported universal household diet, school attendance, medical practice or toilet design established. Land edicts describe prescriptions and domestic production; elite tomb service objects do not prove population-wide sanitation. Most food-related evidence is agricultural property, not recipes. The iron lion’s lost bronze rider and temple are art-historical interpretations. Source access limits preserved in notes.
